Show that every term of bn=(1+1n)nb_n = \left(1+\frac1n\right)^nbn​=(1+n1​)n is rational, and explain why its irrational limit eee is another "hole" in Q\mathbb{Q}Q.

bn=(n+1n)n∈Q,lim⁡n→∞bn=e∉Qb_n = \left(\frac{n+1}{n}\right)^n \in \mathbb{Q}, \qquad \lim_{n\to\infty} b_n = e \notin \mathbb{Q}bn​=(nn+1​)n∈Q,n→∞lim​bn​=e∈/Q
Show proof
  1. bn=(n+1n)nb_n = \left(\frac{n+1}{n}\right)^nbn​=(nn+1​)n with n+1n\frac{n+1}{n}nn+1​ rational. A rational number raised to a positive integer power is rational, so bn∈Qb_n \in \mathbb{Q}bn​∈Q for every nnn.
  2. The sequence (bn)(b_n)(bn​) is increasing and bounded above (taken as known — it is standard), hence convergent. Its limit is called eee.
  3. That e∉Qe \notin \mathbb{Q}e∈/Q is an established theorem (proved, for instance, by estimating the remainder of e=∑k=0∞1k!e = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{k!}e=∑k=0∞​k!1​). So the rational sequence (bn)(b_n)(bn​) converges to no rational number — another hole in Q\mathbb{Q}Q, distinct from the one at 2\sqrt22​.

Prove that the Babylonian sequence (xn)(x_n)(xn​) is Cauchy but has no limit in Q\mathbb{Q}Q — this is what completeness is about.

∣xm−xn∣→0  (m,n→∞),∄ r∈Q:xn→r|x_m - x_n| \to 0 \ \ (m,n \to \infty), \qquad \nexists\, r \in \mathbb{Q} : x_n \to r∣xm​−xn​∣→0  (m,n→∞),∄r∈Q:xn​→r
Show proof
  1. From the error analysis, en+1≤en28e_{n+1} \leq \frac{e_n^2}{8}en+1​≤8en2​​ with e1=14e_1 = \frac14e1​=41​. Since en≤2−ne_n \leq 2^{-n}en​≤2−n by induction (true at n=1n=1n=1, and en+1≤2−2n8=2−(2n+3)≤2−(n+1)e_{n+1} \leq \frac{2^{-2n}}{8} = 2^{-(2n+3)} \leq 2^{-(n+1)}en+1​≤82−2n​=2−(2n+3)≤2−(n+1)), we get en→0e_n \to 0en​→0. With ∣xn−2∣=enxn+2≤en2|x_n-\sqrt2| = \frac{e_n}{x_n+\sqrt2} \leq \frac{e_n}{2}∣xn​−2​∣=xn​+2​en​​≤2en​​, we have xn→2x_n \to \sqrt2xn​→2​ as real numbers.
  2. Hence ∣xm−xn∣≤∣xm−2∣+∣xn−2∣|x_m - x_n| \leq |x_m - \sqrt2| + |x_n - \sqrt2|∣xm​−xn​∣≤∣xm​−2​∣+∣xn​−2​∣ becomes arbitrarily small for large m,nm, nm,n: (xn)(x_n)(xn​) is a Cauchy sequence.
  3. If xn→rx_n \to rxn​→r for some rational rrr, uniqueness of limits forces r=2r = \sqrt2r=2​. But 2∉Q\sqrt2 \notin \mathbb{Q}2​∈/Q — a contradiction. So (xn)(x_n)(xn​) has no limit inside Q\mathbb{Q}Q.
  4. For reference, the classical proof that 2∉Q\sqrt2 \notin \mathbb{Q}2​∈/Q: if 2=pq\sqrt2 = \frac pq2​=qp​ in lowest terms, then p2=2q2p^2 = 2q^2p2=2q2, so ppp is even; writing p=2kp = 2kp=2k gives q2=2k2q^2 = 2k^2q2=2k2, so qqq is even too — contradicting lowest terms.
